summary: Automated valuation is the sector's oldest deployed AI, and it is now formally regulated: federal quality-control standards for AVMs took effect in 2025. Valuation, leasing automation, 3D capture, and property operations are where AI actually runs; the regulator record and the platforms' own model documentation are the sources.

analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 28.9% of firms in real estate and rental and leasing reported using AI in the most recent period, up from 28.0% the prior period, placing the sector in a measurable and gradually rising adoption band. That figure covers the full NAICS 53 grouping, so it blends large institutional operators with small landlords and independent brokers, meaning actual deployment intensity at the enterprise level is likely considerably higher than the headline share suggests.

The most established and consequential AI application in the sector is automated valuation. Zillow publishes Zestimate valuations for more than 110 million homes using a neural network model that draws on county and tax assessor records, MLS feeds, listing signals, and user-submitted data, with updates running multiple times per week. HouseCanary offers AI-powered valuations and forecasts covering over 136 million U.S. properties, combining machine learning with image recognition that identifies room types and assesses home condition from photographs. Opendoor takes valuation a step further by placing its pricing models at direct balance-sheet risk, having used algorithmic offers to purchase homes from over 308,082 homeowners. On the commercial side, Prophia applies document AI to lease abstraction, extracting key terms and rent-roll obligations from commercial leases and combining machine output with expert validation to produce structured portfolio data.

Operational automation is advancing on several fronts. EliseAI deploys agentic conversational AI that handles leasing inquiries, schedules tours, follows up with prospects, and manages maintenance requests around the clock, positioning the platform as more than a chatbot and as a full workflow automation layer for property management. Building Engines, a JLL company, offers its Prism platform to commercial property teams with AI-driven recommendations and automation designed to cut costs and grow net operating income. Matterport digitizes physical buildings into 3D models, integrating with platforms such as Procore and Autodesk to reduce site visits and support portfolio management decisions with spatial data. Compass integrates AI into residential brokerage workflows, while JLL has stated it has invested more in AI technology than any other real estate company, applying it across brokerage, facilities management, and portfolio analytics.

The regulatory environment has sharpened significantly around valuation models. The CFPB, FHFA, OCC, Federal Reserve Board, FDIC, and NCUA jointly finalized a rule implementing quality control standards for automated valuation models used by mortgage originators and secondary market issuers to determine collateral worth on consumer principal dwellings. Under that rule, institutions must adopt policies and control systems ensuring AVMs meet standards for confidence in estimates, protection against data manipulation, avoidance of conflicts of interest, and random sample testing. This is the first binding federal framework specifically targeting the sector's oldest and most widely deployed AI, and it applies directly to any institution using AVMs in credit decisions or securitization determinations.

On the investment and community side, CRETI maintains a network of over 500 investors focused on real estate technology and runs a zero-equity accelerator for emerging proptech companies, making it a useful barometer of where early-stage capital concentrates. NAR REACH, created by Second Century Ventures, operates as the residential proptech accelerator through which the National Association of Realtors vets and scales technology tools for agents and brokerages. CREtech convenes the commercial proptech market, with its New York conference drawing approximately 3,000 leaders and facilitating over 20,000 pre-scheduled meetings, giving a reasonable read on where enterprise adoption conversations are actually happening.

For a decision-maker weighing deployment, the sourced material points to a sector where AI in valuation is no longer optional infrastructure but regulated infrastructure, requiring compliance with federal quality control standards if the models touch mortgage decisions. The operational automation case, particularly in leasing communications and building management, appears to rest on cost reduction and staff reallocation rather than on published ROI figures, as the sources describe efficiency and NOI improvement in directional terms without disclosing specific benchmarks. The gap between the Census adoption rate and the activity visible at the enterprise tier suggests that smaller operators have meaningful room to catch up, while larger players are already competing partly on the sophistication of their AI stack.
